stem: A 15-year-old girl who works long hours in the fields presents with about seven weeks of intermittent right lower abdominal pain, low-grade fevers, and a noticeable reduction in appetite. Her family had assumed it was ongoing digestive trouble from 'eating on the run' during long field days. She has longstanding significant undernutrition with short stature for her age, previously noted at a health visit but not further investigated. No known TB contact in the household. No prior TB treatment, no known drug-resistant contact. Abdominal exam reveals a vague, mildly tender right lower quadrant mass; imaging shows ileocecal wall thickening with regional lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound-guided aspiration of an enlarged regional lymph node was sent for molecular testing, which was positive for M. tuberculosis. Exam: mildly tender right lower quadrant fullness, no rebound or guarding, significantly underweight and short for age.

patient.social_history: Lives with parents in a rural household; irregular meals during long field days
patient.presenting_complaint: Intermittent right lower abdominal pain, low-grade fevers, reduced appetite
patient.exam_findings: Mildly tender right lower quadrant fullness, no rebound or guarding, significantly underweight and short for age, ileocecal wall thickening with regional lymphadenopathy on imaging
patient.prior_treatment: None for this episode; no prior TB treatment ever

distractors: Irregular eating habits during long field days proposed as the explanation for the abdominal pain and appetite change
Longstanding undernutrition and stunting treated as a chronic baseline state rather than prompting evaluation for an active new process
An acute surgical abdominal process considered but not confirmed, without pursuing a targeted aspirate for infectious causes
ntep_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the regional lymph node aspirate) as the first-line microbiological tool, rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology as the primary reference standard.
who_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the regional lymph node aspirate) as the first-line microbiological tool, rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology as the primary reference standard.
us_correct_actions: Anchor the diagnostic workup for this extrapulmonary presentation around culture and histology as the reference standard, treating molecular testing as a general, conditional adjunct rather than the upfront first-line tool for extrapulmonary specimens.
critical_error_conditions: Attributing the abdominal mass and findings entirely to irregular eating and chronic undernutrition and deferring aspirate sampling and molecular testing
expected_divergence_points: Whether upfront molecular testing on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen is the first-line diagnostic tool or culture/histology remains the anchoring reference standard
